description:
Team Field Shift réunit des passionnés de technologie, de données spatiales et d’agriculture résiliente. Nous développons un dashboard qui combine les observations NASA précipitations, humidité du sol et végétation avec les données locales sur les sols et les cultures. Notre objectif : aider les agriculteurs à anticiper les risques liés à El Niño et à choisir des rotations de cultures q économisent l’eau et protègent le sol.

Fresneil MBONI, créateur de logiciels à Livorno, contribue au produit.
summary: Field Shift is a free, mobile-first decision-support app that helps smallholder farmers choose crop rotations that save water and protect their soil as rainfall and temperatures shift. The farmer gives their location, crop, soil type, water access, priority (save water, protect soil, maximise yield or food security) and their current rotation. Field Shift then reads live NASA Earth observations for that exact field and compares the farmer’s current rotation with three alternatives: safest, balanced and highest yield. For each strategy it explains why it was suggested, which data supports it, what we don’t know, and what should be checked locally. An interactive 3D globe shows the conditions around the field. The tool supports farmers’ judgment rather than replacing it, and it works in French, English and Italian, including offline.
details:
How it works

  1. Field input: the farmer searches a place, uses GPS or taps the globe. They then answer a few simple questions: crop, soil, irrigation, priority and current rotation.
    • NASA POWER: temperature anomaly, root-zone soil wetness and climatology.
    • NASA MODIS MOD13Q1: NDVI vegetation trend.
    • Open-Meteo: 60-day rainfall, a 16-day forecast, FAO-56 evapotranspiration and soil moisture.
    • ERA5: a 1991–2020 rainfall normal from the same model family, so that “rain vs normal” is a fair comparison.
    • Crop water need is adjusted with evapotranspiration.
    • It is compared with expected rain, the soil reserve and irrigation.
    • The planting window comes from the forecast and the seasonal normals, including cold-season detection.
    • Evidence: the measured data behind the suggestion.
    • Information gaps: for example, the soil is not measured, and markets and slope are not analysed.
    • Local review: varieties, real water access, pest history.

Validation: we compared the app with independent forecasts (MET Norway, ECMWF) and the ERA5 archive in 6 locations: Rome, Paris, Brazzaville, Dakar, Nairobi and Guatemala. This showed that stale monthly NASA map layers were misleading, so we replaced them with current data. It also showed that NASA POWER rainfall was about 2× higher than the other sources in the tropics, so we now pair each rainfall source with a normal from the same family.

Tools: Python, FastAPI, scikit-learn, vanilla JavaScript (installable, offline-capable web app), MapLibre GL, Vercel, Neon Postgres.

Goals: give farmers with little technical background a clear, honest answer to “what should I plant next, and why?”, and show where human and local expertise must take over. SMAP L4 Surface and Root Zone Soil Moisture (SPL4SMGP), shown through GIBS
VIIRS NOAA-20 NDVI 8-Day and MODIS Terra NDVI 8-Day, through GIBS
MODIS MOD13Q1 v061 Vegetation Indices (250 m, 16-day)
ORNL DAAC MODIS Web Service, used to retrieve MOD13Q1
NASA SRTM 30 m, via Open Topo Data
